In 1953, Lord Simon of Wythenshawe, who had been BBC chair for five years, summed up the strange paradox of the charter. He dismissed it as a long, “almost bewilderingly vague” document “containing masses of legalistic material which is of no use to any governor in normal times”. And yet, he continued, it has just about worked: “The intentions of successive governments have been well understood by the BBC”, while the BBC has maintained something close to “full freedom and responsibility for their work”.

This strange, flawed process seems to have survived for a century not because it is perfect, or even particularly good, but because no one has yet come up with something better. So again and again, hundreds of thousands of people try to conjure up the BBC they want; one which won’t make the same mistakes, which will reflect the version of Britain that they want to see. And every time the BBC reappears, as though its existence were never in doubt.

“This will be the most important charter negotiation in the history of the BBC,” John Shield, a former director of communications at the BBC, told me. “But then, they always are.”
